claims.text: The hierarchical heterostructure contains nanoscale precipitates.
The hierarchical heterostructure contains phase boundaries and localized heterogeneities.
High-resolution electron microscopy and digital image correlation can provide microstructural descriptors suitable for training the proposed machine-learning models.
The machine-learning models can predict local elastic parameters from the extracted descriptors.
The machine-learning models can predict local yield parameters from the extracted descriptors.
Predicted local parameters can serve as inputs to a multiscale framework that simulates tensile and fracture tests.
Spatial microstructural variability can be mapped to local mechanical parameters by the machine-learning model.
The integrated framework homogenizes atomic-scale information while preserving mechanically important heterogeneity.
Preserving critical heterogeneity while homogenizing atomic-scale information enables rapid prediction of global mechanical properties.
The proposed framework can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of hierarchically heterogeneous HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 20–30% relative to established full-scale simulations.
The proposed framework will reduce computational simulation time by up to approximately 70% relative to established full-scale simulations.
The framework can operate over approximately 25–400 °C under standardized tensile and fracture test environments.
Model performance may fail or degrade when evaluated microstructures lie outside the training-data distribution.
Extreme strain rates, very high temperatures, or unusual defect configurations may activate deformation mechanisms absent from the model.
Prediction errors consistently exceeding 30% across multiple tests are declared to falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of the machine-learning component to generalize across the observed microstructures is declared to falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The framework is called 'continuum-to-atomistic upscaling,' while the described operation homogenizes atomic-scale or local information into global continuum behavior. That operation is ordinarily atomistic-to-continuum upscaling, so the stated direction of scale transfer is internally inconsistent.
